subtype: Approach: suppressing emotion to seem strong [Pitfall]
passage: Binita didi asked me to tell it the way it happened. So: when Papa died, my uncle put a hand on my shoulder, his own eyes wet, and said, “Now you're the man of our home, no crying.” I was fourteen. I wiped my face and never cried in front of anyone again. I swept the floor, carried the groceries, and studied until two at night so that Amma would see one thing going right. For three weeks I felt nothing, which I took for strength. Then I shouted at my little sister for spilling water, really shouted, and after that I couldn't sleep. I lay awake with my heart racing for no reason. I'm Pranav, and what I know now is that the crying I didn't do didn't disappear. It waited.

qa.q: What did Pranav's uncle say to him?
qa.a: Pranav's uncle said, Now you're the man of our home, no crying.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling during the three weeks before he shouted?
qa.a: Pranav felt numb, which he took for strength, while the grief stayed hidden inside.

qa.q: What could Pranav have done differently?
qa.a: Pranav could have let himself cry and talked with family or a counsellor, so the grief could be expressed instead of waiting.

qa.q: How might Pranav's little sister have felt when he shouted?
qa.a: Pranav's little sister was probably startled and hurt, since she could not know the reason behind the shouting.

grounding: A boy told to be the man of the house hides his tears and throws himself into chores and study, and weeks later has outbursts and sleeplessness.

subtype: Approach: suppressing emotion to seem strong [Pitfall]
passage: I live across the corridor from Nilesh's family, so I saw more than I was meant to. At his father's funeral, an uncle gripped Nilesh's shoulder and said, "You're the man of this house now. No crying." Nilesh nodded. He didn't cry once that I saw. For weeks after, he was everywhere: fixing the leaking tap, fetching gas cylinders, carrying his sister Charu's school bag, studying at the window till one in the morning. People in the building said, "So strong, that boy." Then, a month later, I heard shouting through the wall. Nilesh had thrown his geometry box at the door because Charu used his ruler. Charu was crying. After that his light stayed on all night, most nights. I don't know what was going on inside him. But he didn't look strong. He looked like someone holding his breath.

qa.q: What did the uncle say to Nilesh at the funeral?
qa.a: You're the man of this house now. No crying.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have been feeling under all the busyness?
qa.a: Nilesh was probably grieving hard and under great pressure, keeping the sadness in until it burst out as anger and sleepless nights.

qa.q: What would you change first to help Nilesh?
qa.a: An adult could tell Nilesh plainly that crying is allowed, share the chores, and bring in a school counsellor, so the grief has somewhere to go.

qa.q: How is Charu affected by Nilesh holding everything in?
qa.a: Charu gets the outburst over a ruler and ends up crying, so the hidden grief spills onto her too.

grounding: Shows a boy told to be the man of the house hiding his tears in chores and study, and weeks later showing outbursts and sleepless nights.

passage:
Day of the funeral. Dadaji put a heavy hand on Hemant's back. "You're the man of this family now. Men don't cry in front of others." Hemant swallowed hard and went to arrange the chairs. That night he ironed his school uniform and did two chapters of physics.
Three weeks later. Hemant had not missed a single homework, but in class he snapped at Rahul for borrowing his eraser, then stared at the desk, shocked at himself. Sabina Ma'am noticed the dark circles.
Five weeks later. He had barely slept all week. At home he shouted at his little brother over the TV remote and slammed the door so hard a photo frame fell. Papa's photo. He picked it up and couldn't let go. Next morning Sabina Ma'am asked him to stay after class. "I'm fine, Ma'am," he said. "I have to be." She didn't let it go, and that afternoon she called his mother.

qa.q: What did Hemant do on the night of the funeral?
qa.a: He ironed his school uniform and did two chapters of physics.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he couldn't let go of Papa's photo?
qa.a: Hemant was flooded with grief held back for weeks, and the anger and sleeplessness were signs of it.

qa.q: What would you change first for Hemant?
qa.a: Someone in the family could tell Hemant that crying is allowed and share the load, and Sabina Ma'am could connect him with the school counsellor.

qa.q: How does Sabina Ma'am see the changes in Hemant?
qa.a: She notices the dark circles and the snapping, and sees that I'm fine doesn't match what she is watching, so she calls his mother.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who hides his grief to seem strong after his father's death, with outbursts and sleeplessness appearing weeks later.
